summary: Patterns and architectures for coordinating multiple AI agents to solve complex tasks through collaboration

content.overview: Multi-agent orchestration coordinates multiple specialized AI agents to solve complex tasks that exceed single-agent capabilities. Instead of one generalist agent, systems deploy multiple specialist agents (e.g., research agent, coding agent, QA agent) with a coordinator managing collaboration. The 2025 landscape has consolidated around five dominant patterns: centralized orchestration, decentralized coordination, hierarchical structures, event-driven systems, and hybrid human-AI orchestration. Critical tradeoff: Single agents are simpler and cheaper; multi-agent systems handle complexity better but increase cost and coordination overhead.
keyPoints: Core orchestration patterns: (1) Centralized (orchestrator delegates), (2) Decentralized (agents coordinate peer-to-peer), (3) Hierarchical (manager-worker layers), (4) Event-driven (async messaging), (5) Hybrid human-AI
HIERARCHICAL pattern (most common): Orchestrator agent → Specialist agents (Agents as Tools pattern) - top agent acts as manager, delegates to expert sub-agents
CRITICAL: Multi-agent systems cost 2-5x more than single agents (more LLM calls, larger prompts) - only use when task complexity justifies
2025 innovation: 'Puppeteer' orchestrators trained via RL to dynamically sequence agents based on evolving task state (not static workflows)
Event-driven orchestration enables async, resilient systems - agents added/removed without disrupting siblings
Communication mechanisms: (1) Direct (agent-to-agent calls), (2) Shared state/blackboard (common knowledge base), (3) Message queues (async events)
Frameworks: LangGraph (skill/role-based teams), CrewAI (role-based Python teams), AutoGen (Microsoft, research-focused)

examples.title: Hierarchical Agents as Tools Pattern
examples.code:
// Orchestrator Agent:
"I need to research topic X"
  → calls ResearchAgent.search(topic)

"Now analyze the data"
  → calls AnalysisAgent.analyze(data)

"Write a report"
  → calls WriterAgent.generate_report(analysis)
examples.explanation: Top-level orchestrator delegates to specialist agents like a manager delegating to team members

examples.title: Decentralized Collaboration
examples.code:
// Agents coordinate via shared blackboard:
ResearchAgent: Writes findings to shared_state['research']
AnalysisAgent: Reads shared_state['research'], writes to shared_state['analysis']
WriterAgent: Reads shared_state['analysis'], generates report
examples.explanation: Agents coordinate through shared knowledge base without central orchestrator - more autonomous but harder to control

warnings: COST EXPLOSION: Multi-agent systems can easily 3-5x your LLM costs - each agent call, coordination, and handoff consumes tokens
Coordination failures cascade - if agent A's output is wrong, agent B amplifies the error, agent C compounds it further
Debugging multi-agent systems is exponentially harder - trace through multiple agents' reasoning to find root cause
Over-specialization reduces flexibility - narrow agents can't adapt when task requirements shift slightly
Avoid multi-agent for simple tasks - single ReAct agent with tools is faster, cheaper, and simpler for 80% of use cases
Shared state (blackboard pattern) risks race conditions and inconsistency without careful state management
bestPractices: Start with single agent + tools - only move to multi-agent when single agent demonstrably fails on task complexity
Use hierarchical (orchestrator + specialists) for most enterprise use cases - clearer control flow than decentralized
Implement comprehensive logging across ALL agents - track task flow, decisions, handoffs for debugging and auditing
Define clear agent responsibilities with minimal overlap - ambiguity in roles causes coordination failures
Set orchestration timeouts and max handoffs - prevent infinite loops and runaway costs
Consider event-driven patterns for async, long-running workflows (hours/days) instead of synchronous orchestration
